lead: Registration means drawing each virtual object where the real camera sees it. The camera pose has six degrees of freedom: three position values and three orientation values. A tracker must recover that pose in every frame. Three families trade how much world knowledge they assume: a printed marker, natural image features, or SLAM, which builds a map while moving. You meet them in phone AR, museum guides, factory maintenance and surgery overlays.
prereq: You need: 6.1 for registration, Unit 2 for trackers and sensors, and Unit 4 for transformation matrices and yaw, pitch, roll.

sections.h3: Camera pose from a printed marker

blocks.text: A fiducial marker is a printed pattern: a black square with a white border and an inner code. The border gives strong edges; the code gives an ID so several markers can coexist.

items: Convert the frame to grayscale and threshold it; dark marker regions become blobs.
Find contours and fit the four corners of each square candidate.
Warp the square to a front view and check the border and inner code.
Compute the homography H, a 3×3 mapping from the marker plane to the image plane.
Decompose H with camera intrinsics into pose R, t: rotation and translation.
Filter the pose over frames to reduce jitter.

blocks.where: Z is distance in m; f is focal length in pixels; W is marker side in m; w is its width in the image in pixels.

blocks.text: Pose means six degrees of freedom: three position values (x, y, z) and three orientation values (yaw, pitch, roll). Marker size and focal length set the usable range: larger W or longer f gives more pixels w, so pose noise falls. A small, distant marker gives few pixels and noisy depth.

sections.h3: Markerless tracking: features and known models

blocks.text: Markerless tracking does not need a printed target. It uses natural corners and blobs. Detectors such as FAST and ORB find keypoints; descriptors turn the patch around each keypoint into a short code. Matching compares descriptors between frames or against a model. RANSAC (random sample consensus) fits a model from a small random sample, counts inliers, and repeats, so wrong matches are rejected. For a flat surface, a homography is enough. For a known 3D object, Perspective-n-Point (PnP) finds pose from 2D image points matched to 3D model points. Model-based tracking can also follow known edges and contours.

SLAM (simultaneous localisation and mapping) estimates camera pose and a feature map together. The front-end tracks features frame to frame. The map stores 3D feature positions. The back-end optimises poses and map points to reduce error. Loop closure recognises a revisited place and corrects accumulated drift. Relocalisation recovers pose after tracking loss. Visual-inertial odometry fuses camera and IMU, which gives scale and short-term robustness. A single camera has scale ambiguity: the map is correct only up to an unknown factor. Drift grows with distance; anchors, such as a known marker or map point, reduce it. Keep the pipeline and ideas, not the optimisation mathematics.

figure.caption: The curve is Z = f × W ÷ w with f = 800 px and W = 0.08 m, so Z = 64 ÷ w. Both worked markers sit on it: 160 px gives 0.4 m and 2.5 mm depth error, 320 px gives 0.2 m and 0.625 mm, so twice the pixels gives a quarter of the error.

spec.aria: A falling curve of distance against marker width in pixels from 100 to 500, with points at 160 pixels and 0.4 metres and at 320 pixels and 0.2 metres, and a panel working the depth errors 2.5 and 0.625 millimetres.

examples.question: An 80 mm square marker appears 160 pixels wide in a camera with focal length 800 pixels. Find its distance. If one corner is located to ±1 pixel, find the depth error. Repeat when the marker appears 320 pixels wide.
examples.answer: The marker is at 0.4 m with depth error 2.5 mm; at 0.2 m the error is 0.625 mm.
examples.check:
f=800
W=0.08
w1=160
Z1=f*W/w1
err1=Z1*(1/w1)*1000
w2=320
Z2=f*W/w2
err2=Z2*(1/w2)*1000
print(Z1)
print(err1)
print(Z2)
print(err2)

traps: SLAM from one camera does not give an absolute metric pose; scale is unknown unless fused with IMU or anchored.
Marker pose needs camera calibration: focal length and lens distortion. Clean detection alone is not enough.
RANSAC rejects wrong feature matches; it does not smooth jitter. That is the temporal filter.
Homography is for a plane; a full 3D object needs PnP or model-based pose.
Depth from apparent size uses physical marker size W; if W is wrong, Z scales by the same factor.

quiz.q: What are the six degrees of freedom of a pose?
quiz.a: Three position values (x, y, z) and three orientation values (yaw, pitch, roll).

quiz.q: Why does marker tracking threshold the image first?
quiz.a: To separate the dark marker from the background so its edges and corners can be found reliably.

quiz.q: A 100 mm marker appears 200 pixels wide with f = 1000 pixels. Find depth.
Why is depth error smaller when the same marker is closer?
quiz.a: At closer range it covers more pixels w; relative corner error 1/w falls, and depth error Z×(1/w) falls.

quiz.q: What is loop closure in SLAM?
quiz.a: Recognising a previously mapped place and using it to correct drift.

quiz.q: State one difference between homography and PnP.
quiz.a: Homography gives pose for points on a plane; PnP uses 2D-to-3D point matches for a known 3D model.

quiz.q: Why can monocular SLAM not report absolute metres?
quiz.a: It sees only angles and image motion; without a known size, IMU scale, or anchor, the whole map can be scaled without changing the images.

beyond: Not for the exam. Phone AR toolkits hide SLAM behind anchors. Robotics uses visual-inertial SLAM for drones and warehouse robots. Research directions are dense mapping, neural features, and collaborative maps. Search terms: ORB-SLAM, visual-inertial odometry, fiducial marker, PnP RANSAC.
